case_study_insert.main_stem: Sunhill Citrus Packers (SCP) is a private limited company in the agribusiness sector, grading, waxing and exporting citrus fruit for overseas supermarket chains. The company has a workforce of 54 and operates a hierarchical structure with democratic leadership, with founder Rafael Sunhill consulting shift leaders each week. SCP plans to invest $880,000 in an automated grading and waxing line with a cold store, financed by a $520,000 five-year bank loan and $360,000 retained profit. It has fixed costs of $286,000 a year, a variable cost of $6.20 a unit and a selling price of $14.20, and produces 96,000 units a year, where each unit is a graded crate. SCP faces two problems: 8.6% of fruit is rejected for blemishing and absenteeism among graders has reached 11%.
case_study_insert.appendix_1_marketing_ops: Packing and Export Log - Q3 2025: SCP graded 24,600 crates last quarter, of which 8.6% were rejected for blemishing, up from 5.9% a year earlier. Export rejection notices rose to 36 from 22 a month. Average dispatch to the port is 3.4 days. A survey of 700 supermarket produce buyers found 61% would pay up to $0.60 more for waxed grade-A fruit and 49% require a residue-testing certificate before placing orders. A trial of the new optical grader cut rejections to 3.8%. A skills audit found 15 of 54 staff had not completed on-the-job training on the grader; off-the-job training at the provincial college costs $810 per employee.

appendix_2_financial_data.title: Extract from the Statement of Financial Position of Sunhill Citrus Packers as at 31 March 2025 ($ '000)

case_study_insert.appendix_3_external_environment: Economic and Export Bulletin (November 2026): (1) The central bank has raised the base interest rate from 5.0% to 5.75%, increasing the cost of variable-rate borrowing for capital investment. (2) The national minimum wage rises by 7.0% from $13.00 to $13.91 an hour from April 2026, raising packing wages. (3) Fertiliser, wooden crating and freight input costs have risen 11.3% year-on-year, while export citrus prices rose only 2.6% and overseas demand for citrus grew 3.8%.

questions.question_text: SCP plans to fund part of its $880,000 grading line and cold store with a five-year bank loan. Explain two advantages for SCP of using retained profit instead of the loan.
questions.model_answer:
Point 1: Retained profit carries no interest charge and no fixed repayment date, which matters because SCP must cover fixed costs of $286,000 a year from $8.00 contribution per crate ($14.20 − $6.20). Interest on a $520,000 loan would be payable even when the 8.6% rejection rate rises; using the $360,000 already earned keeps cash available to pay the 11%-absence-hit grading team and to fund quality improvements.

Point 2: Internal funds avoid the security and covenants a bank would require, so Rafael Sunhill and the shift leaders can run the new line without lender conditions attached to the cold store. Control stays with the company rather than a creditor. The cost is that $360,000 of reserves is no longer a buffer if export rejection notices keep climbing from 36 a month or freight costs keep rising, leaving SCP reliant on its 96,000-crate output to absorb shocks. Rafael Sunhill could phase the $880,000 project so retained profit funds the grader first and the $520,000 loan is drawn only when the 3.8% export demand growth justifies the cold store.

knowledge_max_2: 1 mark for each valid advantage identified (max 2).
application_analysis_max_6: Up to 3 marks per point for contextual explanation and analysis applied to SCP's costs, reserves and financing.

questions.question_text: SCP wants to win more overseas listings for its graded citrus. Consider hosting buyer visits to the packing house, advertising in an export trade journal, or a social media campaign for consumers. Which should SCP choose? Justify your recommendation.
questions.model_answer:
Buyer visits to the packing house: Inviting supermarket buyers to see the optical grader lets them witness the fall in rejections from 8.6% to 3.8% and inspect the residue-testing process that 49% of buyers require. This builds trust and can secure listings directly, but it is time-consuming, only reaches a few buyers at a time, and diverts managers while the $880,000 line is being commissioned.

Export trade journal advertising: An advert in a specialist journal reaches many produce buyers at once and can carry the 3.8% trial result and the 3.4-day dispatch promise. It is cheaper than hosting visits, but print cannot demonstrate the fruit's quality, and readership may include buyers outside SCP's export markets, so part of the spend is wasted while a $520,000 loan is outstanding.

Social media campaign: A campaign can show the groves, grading and waxing to consumers in importing countries, supporting the 61% who would pay $0.60 more for waxed grade-A fruit and building pull-through for supermarket buyers. Engagement is measurable against the 24,600 crates graded last quarter, but results build slowly and consumer interest does not itself sign an export contract.

Recommendation: SCP should choose buyer visits to the packing house, supported by a small trade journal advert. Visits directly convert the 3.8% trial evidence and residue-testing proof into listings, which is what sells 96,000 crates a year. Journal advertising alone is rejected because print cannot demonstrate quality, and social media is rejected as an indirect consumer channel that cannot close an overseas order while the $520,000 loan must be serviced.

mark_scheme.level_1_1_to_4: Limited outline of the promotional options with minimal application to SCP.
mark_scheme.level_2_5_to_8: Discussion of advantages and disadvantages of at least two options in the context of SCP with some judgement.
mark_scheme.level_3_9_to_12: Detailed discussion of all three options in context with a well-justified recommendation explaining why journal advertising and social media are rejected.

questions.question_text: SCP's absenteeism has reached 11% and 8.6% of fruit is rejected for blemishing. Explain two benefits for SCP of introducing a performance-related bonus for grading staff.
questions.model_answer:
Point 1: A bonus tied to fewer blemished crates gives the workforce of 54 a direct financial reason to handle fruit carefully, which should reduce the 8.6% rejection rate towards the 3.8% achieved with the optical grader and cut the 36 monthly export rejection notices. Because pay depends on quality, staff have an incentive to attend regularly, helping to bring down 11% absenteeism without Rafael Sunhill having to police every shift.

Point 2: A bonus rewards effort more cheaply than permanent wage increases while the 7.0% minimum wage rise takes effect, since it is paid only when the 24,600-crate quarterly target and quality standard are met. Better attendance and fewer rejections protect the $14.20 price and $8.00 contribution needed to service the $520,000 loan. SCP should pilot the bonus on one shift and compare rejection and absence figures with the current baselines before extending it across all 54 staff. The scheme should be reviewed against the 36 monthly rejection notices as well, because a bonus that lifts output without improving quality would waste the $880,000 investment.

knowledge_max_2: 1 mark for each valid benefit identified (max 2).
application_analysis_max_6: Up to 3 marks per point for contextual development linked to SCP's absence rate, rejections, bonus and expansion.

questions.question_text: SCP must train 15 of 54 staff to use the new optical grader. Consider on-the-job training at the packing house or off-the-job training at the provincial college. Which should SCP choose? Justify your decision.
questions.model_answer:
On-the-job training: Instruction at the grader covers SCP's own settings, defect thresholds and cleaning routines, costs no course fees, and keeps the 15 trainees sorting the 24,600 crates packed each quarter. It can cut the 8.6% rejection rate immediately as supervisors correct decisions on real fruit. The disadvantages are that experienced graders lose time coaching, bad habits may spread, and no certificate is issued to prove competence to overseas buyers demanding a residue-testing certificate.

Off-the-job training: The provincial college course costs $810 per employee, so 15 × $810 = $12,150, a small fraction of the $880,000 investment. It gives structured teaching and a formal certificate, valuable when 49% of buyers require documented checks. However, it removes 15 of 54 staff from the line, risking the 3.4-day dispatch to port, and the generic syllabus still needs adapting to SCP's optical equipment.

Decision: SCP should choose on-the-job training at the packing house, with a short certified college module for supervisors. It is cheaper, specific to the installed grader and avoids losing sorting capacity while 11% absenteeism is already disrupting shifts. Full off-the-job training is rejected because the $12,150 fee and lost shifts would slow the 24,600-crate operation and cannot directly reduce the 8.6% rejection rate. A one-shift pilot measured against the 3.8% trial result should decide whether further $810-per-head spending is justified. The board should also weigh the 11% absence rate: training 15 staff is wasted if they are not regularly at work to operate the grader, which is why the bonus scheme should be reviewed alongside the training pilot.

mark_scheme.level_1_1_to_4: Basic description of the two training methods with limited application to SCP.
mark_scheme.level_2_5_to_8: Detailed analysis of the benefits and drawbacks of both methods in the context of SCP.
mark_scheme.level_3_9_to_12: Comprehensive evaluation of both methods with a justified decision covering cost, disruption and relevance to the grader.

questions.question_text: SCP's management wants to use its cost and output data to judge the new grading line. Calculate and explain how that data can be used.

sub_parts.model_answer: Formula: Contribution per unit = Selling price − Variable cost per unit. Substitution: $14.20 − $6.20 = $8.00. Answer: contribution per unit is $8.00.
Formula: Break-even output = Fixed costs ÷ Contribution per unit. Substitution: $286,000 ÷ $8.00 = 35,750 units. Answer: break-even output is 35,750 crates a year.

sub_parts.question_text: Explain four ways SCP's management can use this financial data.
sub_parts.model_answer:
1. With break-even at 35,750 crates and output of 96,000, SCP has a margin of safety of 60,250 crates, so blemishing at 8.6% would have to be far worse before the $286,000 fixed costs are not covered.
2. Contribution of $8.00 lets managers test the survey: the 61% who would pay $0.60 more for waxed grade-A fruit would lift contribution to $8.60, which can be weighed against the extra waxing cost before export pricing is set.
3. Average total cost of $9.18 a crate ($286,000 ÷ 96,000 = $2.98, plus $6.20) is a benchmark for the $880,000 line: grading must cut the 8.6% rejection rate or raise throughput if unit cost is to fall.
4. The figures guide financing: with 60,250 crates of cushion, managers can judge whether interest on the $520,000 loan is affordable while 11% absenteeism is tackled, and compare that with spending $810 per employee on training 15 staff.

questions.model_answer: (i) Contribution per unit = $8.00 | (ii) Break-even output = 35,750 crates | (iii) Four contextual uses explained: 60,250-crate safety margin against 8.6% rejections; $0.60 premium on $8.00 contribution; $9.18 unit-cost benchmark for the new line; and loan affordability versus $810 training cost.

working_marks: 1 mark for correct formula/method, 1 mark for accurate numerical answer in (i) and (ii). 1 mark per valid applied point in (iii).

questions.question_text: Using Appendix 2, evaluate SCP's liquidity by calculating the current ratio and the acid test ratio for 2024 and 2025. Has SCP's financial position improved? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer:
Calculations:
Current Ratio 2024 = 1.50 : 1
Current Ratio 2025 = 1.72 : 1
Acid Test Ratio 2024 = 0.92 : 1
Acid Test Ratio 2025 = 1.16 : 1

Detailed workings: 2024 current assets = $210,000 inventories + $260,000 trade receivables + $70,000 cash = $540,000, and 2025 current assets = $190,000 + $298,000 + $96,000 = $584,000. Dividing by current liabilities gives $540,000 ÷ $360,000 = 1.50 and $584,000 ÷ $340,000 = 1.72. Excluding inventories: ($540,000 − $210,000) ÷ $360,000 = $330,000 ÷ $360,000 = 0.92, and ($584,000 − $190,000) ÷ $340,000 = $394,000 ÷ $340,000 = 1.16.

Evaluation: Short-term liquidity improved on both measures. Current liabilities fell from $360,000 to $340,000 while current assets rose from $540,000 to $584,000, helped by cash rising from $70,000 to $96,000. The stricter test, which removes fruit stock that can spoil or be rejected, climbed from 0.92 to 1.16, so SCP can now cover short-term debts from cash and receivables without depending on the $190,000 of inventory. This matters while the company commits $360,000 of retained profit and borrows $520,000 for the $880,000 line. The reservation is that receivables rose from $260,000 to $298,000, so overseas supermarket chains are holding more of SCP's cash, and 11% absenteeism plus 8.6% rejections could raise costs faster than the ratio gain implies.

Conclusion: SCP's financial position has improved. Both measures rose and the 1.16 figure shows the improvement does not rely on unsold stock, giving more headroom to meet bills. Rising receivables are the main risk, so Rafael Sunhill should tighten credit terms with overseas buyers before drawing more of the $520,000 loan.

mark_scheme.level_1_1_to_4: States figures or changes without accurate ratio calculations.
mark_scheme.level_2_5_to_8: Accurately calculates the current ratio and acid test ratio for both years with contextual analysis of the trend.
mark_scheme.level_3_9_to_12: Accurate calculations for both years with detailed evaluation of inventory, receivables and liability movements and a justified conclusion on whether liquidity improved.

questions.question_text: Explain one advantage and one disadvantage for SCP of offering waxed grade-A fruit with a residue-testing certificate to overseas buyers.
questions.model_answer:
Advantage: The survey found that 49% of 700 produce buyers require a residue-testing certificate and 61% would pay $0.60 more for waxed grade-A fruit, so the offer can secure listings and lift contribution above $8.00 a crate, helping recover the $880,000 line. It also addresses export rejection notices that have risen to 36 a month, protecting the 24,600-crate quarterly volume.

Disadvantage: Testing and certification add per-crate costs and paperwork, raising the $6.20 variable cost or $286,000 fixed costs, and the 61% premium is an intention in a survey, not a guaranteed payment. Waxing also cannot remove blemishes, so if the optical grader fails to cut the 8.6% rejection rate the certificate will simply document more failures. The insert gives no testing cost, so the net gain cannot be quantified and SCP should trial the offer with one buyer first. It should compare the premiums actually received and the 36 monthly rejection notices before extending certification to all 700 surveyed buyers' orders.

knowledge_max_2: 1 mark for a valid advantage and 1 mark for a valid disadvantage.
application_analysis_max_6: Up to 3 marks per point for contextual development linked to SCP's survey, certificate, rejection rate and costs.

questions.question_text: Using Appendix 3, evaluate how the interest rate rise to 5.75%, the 7.0% minimum wage increase and the 11.3% rise in fertiliser, crating and freight costs will affect SCP. Which change will have the greatest impact? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer:
Interest rate rise (5.0% to 5.75%): If the $520,000 five-year loan is variable-rate, the 0.75 percentage-point rise adds 0.75% × $520,000 = $3,900 a year to interest. That is modest beside $286,000 of fixed costs and can be capped by fixing the rate, so the direct effect is small. The indirect effect is that dearer credit makes the $880,000 grading line more expensive to refinance and raises the cost of any further borrowing.

Minimum wage increase (7.0%, from $13.00 to $13.91): Each grading hour costs $0.91 more (7.0% × $13.00 = $0.91). The insert gives no hours worked and no individual pay rates, so an annual wage total would be invented; the defensible test is that 11% absenteeism forces repeated cover, and unless productivity holds near 96,000 crates from a workforce of 54, unit labour cost rises and the $8.00 contribution falls.

Input costs (up 11.3%): Fertiliser, crating and freight feed the $6.20 variable cost on every crate. The insert does not decompose that cost, so only a labelled upper bound is honest: if the whole $6.20 were exposed, 11.3% × $6.20 = $0.70 a crate, and at 96,000 crates that is roughly $67,300 a year (96,000 × $0.7006). Even a smaller exposed share cuts the $8.00 contribution on every crate, and export prices rose only 2.6%, so little can be passed on.

Conclusion: The 11.3% input-cost rise will have the greatest impact. It recurs across all 96,000 crates and directly erodes the $8.00 contribution that repays the $520,000 loan and funds the $880,000 expansion, whereas interest adds only $3,900 a year and can be fixed. The wage rise is second because it recurs with each replacement, but a bonus can offset part of it. SCP should cut the 8.6% rejection rate and seek the $0.60 grade-A premium rather than absorb the whole increase.

mark_scheme.level_1_1_to_4: Identifies the external changes with limited application to SCP.
mark_scheme.level_2_5_to_8: Analyses the impact of at least two changes on SCP's costs, prices or finance in context.
mark_scheme.level_3_9_to_12: Detailed evaluation of all three changes with a justified judgement that input-cost inflation has the greatest impact and why the others are smaller.
